plain_text:
I was born in Cuba, and I spent the first eight and a half
years of my life there. After the Cuban Revolution, my
parents decided that they didn't want to risk staying there,
so in 1960, we immigrated to the United States. I guess my
journey starts there because as a Cuban American, I'm an
immigrant and I'm a minority individual. We moved to
Pittsburgh, where I learned English.
semantic_text: I was born in Cuba, and I spent the first eight and a half years of my life there. After the Cuban Revolution, my parents decided that they didn't want to risk staying there, so in 1960, we immigrated to the United States. I guess my journey starts there because as a Cuban American, I'm an immigrant and I'm a minority individual. We moved to Pittsburgh, where I learned English.

plain_text:
The second big thing is that I became a physician.


My father was a physician, but he never really pushed

it on me. I think I opted for medicine because it was a

noble profession and I would always have a job.

The second big thing is that I became a physician.

plain_text:
I was originally a history major in college, and I always
had a strong interest in politics and current affairs,
particularly around Latin America but in the United States
as well. I quickly realized if I wanted to be a physician—and
a good one—I wouldn't have time for much else. Medical
residency brought me to the West Coast, and I went to the
University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), for training
in primary care general internal medicine. I fell in love with
the area and lived in San Francisco for 37 years, where I
built my career.

Medical residency brought me to the West Coast, and I went to the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), for training in primary care general internal medicine. I fell in love with the area and lived in San Francisco for 37 years, where I built my career.

plain_text:
I learned research methods during a two-year [clinical]
fellowship, which turned me on to academic research.
There were people around me who encouraged and
supported me. Dr. Steve Schroeder [Director of the UCSF
Division of General Internal Medicine] was a mentor
and my first boss at UCSF. He was an influential leader
in general internal medicine, which didn't really exist in
many academic centers at the time.

plain_text:
I began to collaborate with behavioral and social
scientists. I worked first on depression prevention
in primary care and in tobacco use and smoking
cessation among Latinos, and then moved more
toward population science.

plain_text:
A lot of my clinical work had very little to do with my
research. I got funding from NIH very early on, but I also
really enjoyed my role as a leader in research and as a
clinician, a generalist, and an educator at UCSF.
